implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines realises the fan-out with async inside a coroutineScope and the barrier with awaitAll, which the API documents as resuming with the whole list of values (or the first exception, immediately); the aggregation is then a fold over that list, so the list index is the correlation state and the scope guarantees no part outlives the composite. The classic coordinator object only returns when parts cross a broker; in-process the coroutine scope is the entire composed processor.
pitfalls: awaitAll propagates the first exception and cancels the scope; a partial aggregate needs supervisorScope plus per-async runCatching.
async without an explicit dispatcher inherits the caller's, so a blocking part on Dispatchers.Default starves the pool - switch to Dispatchers.IO for blocking work.
Dropping the coroutineScope and using GlobalScope.async detaches the parts from the composite: awaitAll can no longer cancel them.

variants.name: Flow.flatMapMerge for streaming parts
variants.implementation_notes: Flow.flatMapMerge is the streaming form when parts arrive as a flow rather than as one message: the transform returns a flow per part and flatMapMerge merges them with an explicit concurrency limit (the API page describes it as a shortcut for map(transform).flattenMerge(concurrency) and calls it a merging, experimental operator that most application flows do not need). The aggregate is a fold over the merged emissions, so it must be order-independent or reassemble by part index.
pitfalls: flatMapMerge interleaves emissions, so a merge that assumes arrival order produces wrong composites - key parts by index and reassemble.
A failing inner flow fails the whole collection unless the per-part flow catches; with flatMapMerge the failure also cancels the sibling parts' collection.
The operator is marked @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi; pinning kotlinx-coroutines and opting in explicitly keeps the composed processor from breaking on upgrades.
